questions.text: An architect presents their work in a professional magazine and receives media recognition for innovative design. Later, the architect uses this publication to support a claim of 'recognized expertise in innovative residential design.' This claim is:

options.text: Valid because the magazine is a recognized publication with a wide readership and industry influence
Valid because the recognition came from external sources, not self-promotion, and is documented
Invalid unless the recognition reflects 'professional consensus' established through 'years of experience' per §1-f
Valid as long as the architect does not pay the magazine or engage in any form of compensation for the feature

rationale.a: Publication prestige does not fulfill the Code's specific requirement for professional consensus and academic/experience backing. [cite: 98]
rationale.b: External recognition is valuable, but the Code requires specialization claims to be substantiated facts sanctioned by the profession. [cite: 98]
rationale.d: The prohibition is on exaggerated or misleading publicity; the lack of payment doesn't make an unsubstantiated specialization claim valid. [cite: 98, 126]
rationale.correct: Specialization claims require professional consensus and substantiated years of experience; individual media recognition is not equivalent to professional consensus. [cite: 90, 98]
rationale.takeaway: Misrepresenting qualifications by claiming specialization without substantiated professional consensus is an ethical violation. [cite: 90, 94, 98]

questions.text: An architect is designing a residential building in a flood-prone area. The client requests cost reduction by eliminating required flood mitigation measures. The architect should:

options.text: Comply with the client's request to maintain the project, even if it means ignoring safety protocols
Advise the client against the cost-reduction measure because it compromises public safety, even if this risks losing the commission
Let the structural engineer make the decision about safety measures, as they are more qualified to assess the risks involved
Include a disclaimer in the plans stating the client rejected safety measures, thereby transferring liability to the client

rationale.a: Complying with unsafe requests violates the primary duty to the public and potential legal liability requirements. [cite: 89, 112]
rationale.c: The architect bears primary responsibility for overall design safety and must actively advise against unsafe decisions. [cite: 89]
rationale.d: Disclaimers do not absolve an architect from their ethical duty to protect the safety and well-being of the community. [cite: 112]
rationale.correct: The architect must advise the client against projects or measures that are impractical or unsafe, prioritizing public welfare over the loss of a commission. [cite: 89, 112, 118]
rationale.takeaway: Public safety (Obligation 1) is the highest priority; client preferences that compromise that safety must be refused. [cite: 112, 118]

questions.text: A registered architect learns that a retired engineer has been preparing architectural drawings and charging clients architectural fees, claiming 'equivleant qualifications from engineering experience.' Under §1-c and RA 9266 §29, the appropriate analysis is:

options.text: No violation exists because the engineer has extensive building experience, which is often considered equivalent
Violation exists only if the engineer signs documents as 'Architect', which would mislead clients
Violation exists because unauthorized practice of architecture is illegal under RA 9266 §29; the architect must report to the Board regardless of how the engineer labels themselves
The architect should only intervene if a client complains, as it is not their responsibility to monitor others

rationale.a: Experience in related fields does not substitute for the legal requirement of registration to practice architecture. [cite: 85, 90]
rationale.b: The performance of architectural services for a fee by an unregistered individual is illegal regardless of the title used. [cite: 85, 90]
rationale.d: The obligation to report illegal practice is independent of whether a specific client complaint has been filed. [cite: 90, 97]
rationale.correct: Section 1-c requires architects to abide by laws and not act detrimentally to the profession; silence about unlicensed practice violates this duty. Under RA 9266, practicing architecture without registration is illegal. [cite: 85, 90, 97]
rationale.takeaway: Illegal practice is determined by the work performed, not the title used; reporting is a mandatory professional obligation. [cite: 90, 111]

questions.text: A building material manufacturer offers an architect a 15% commission for every specification of their product in a design. Under Section 4-b, the architect's response should be:

options.text: Accept the commission as legitimate additional income, provided it is disclosed to the client
Decline the commission; accept only market discount credited to the client
Accept if the material is genuinely appropriate for the project and aligns with the client's best interests
Request a flat fee instead of percentage-based commission to avoid conflicts of interest

rationale.a: Receiving hidden commissions is a violation of the sole-compensation rule and creates an unethical conflict of interest. [cite: 158, 161, 205]
rationale.c: Material appropriateness does not justify receiving commissions; the incentive creates an unethical reciprocal relationship that compromises objectivity. [cite: 161, 166, 213]
rationale.d: Any form of remuneration from interested sources other than the client is prohibited, whether flat or percentage-based. [cite: 169, 172, 205]
rationale.correct: Section 4-b prohibits receiving commissions or favors from firms handling building materials; any market discount obtained must be fully credited to the client. [cite: 119, 205, 207]
rationale.takeaway: Compensation must come only from the client; benefits from manufacturers must be transferred to the client to avoid bias. [cite: 119, 158, 205]

questions.text: An architect claims to specialize in 'sustainable hospital design' based on three years of experience with hospital projects. According to Section 1-f, what is the violation?

options.text: The architect cannot claim any specialization in hospital design without formal certification
The architect's specialization claim lacks the 'well-known facts' and 'years of experience' required by professional consensus
Architects are prohibited from having specializations unless recognized by a governing body
The claim is valid as long as the architect has completed at least one hospital project and has relevant continuing education

rationale.a: Specialization is allowed, but only when substantiated by experience and consensus as required by the Code. [cite: 98]
rationale.c: The Code does not prohibit specializations; it regulates how they are claimed and substantiated to prevent public misrepresentation. [cite: 98]
rationale.d: A single project or limited experience (3 years) is insufficient to establish recognized expertise according to professional standards. [cite: 90, 98]
rationale.correct: Section 1-f requires that professional specializations are 'well known facts or sanctioned by professional consensus and years of experience.' Claims must be substantiated by academic credentials or a recognized track record. [cite: 90, 98]
rationale.takeaway: Specializations require documented expertise AND professional consensus. It is an ethical violation to misrepresent or falsify professional qualifications. [cite: 90, 94, 98]

questions.text: Under the Code of Ethical Conduct, which of the following is the architect's PRIMARY responsibility to the public?

options.text: To maximize project profitability, ensuring financial success for stakeholders
To advance the safety, health, and well-being of people and the community
To prioritize client preferences in all decisions, even if it conflicts with public interest
To minimize construction costs, focusing on budget constraints over quality

rationale.a: This confuses business objectives with professional obligations. Maximizing profit cannot override the Code's mandate to advance public safety and welfare—profit is subordinate to public interest. [cite: 89, 112]
rationale.c: This reverses the hierarchy of obligations. While client service is important, public welfare takes priority; an architect must refuse client requests that compromise safety. [cite: 89, 112, 118]
rationale.d: Like option a, this prioritizes cost reduction over the Code's explicit requirement to advance public health and safety. [cite: 89, 112]
rationale.correct: Code §1-a establishes that the architect 'shall seek opportunities to be of constructive service... and advance the safety, health and well-being of the people and the community.' This obligation supersedes all other considerations. [cite: 89, 96, 112]
rationale.takeaway: Public welfare is the highest obligation. Remember: Safety > Client > Profit. [cite: 112, 118]

questions.text: An architect with 12 years of experience in commercial office design is offered a hospital project. The architect has completed three hospital projects under another architect's supervision but has never been the architect-of-record for a hospital. Which characterization of the architect's qualifications is MOST ACCURATE per §1-f?

options.text: The architect can claim 'hospital design specialization' due to 12 years of practice experience, which demonstrates a broad understanding of architectural principles
The architect can claim 'hospital design specialization' based on three completed hospital projects, showcasing practical experience in the field

The architect cannot claim hospital design specialization; only that the architect 'has experience with hospital projects'—which lacks the professional consensus and independent responsibility required by §1-f
The architect can claim any specialization after 10 years of practice, regardless of focus areas, as long as they have a comprehensive portfolio

rationale.a: Practice years in one sector do not translate to recognized expertise in another specialized sector without substantiation. [cite: 98]
rationale.b: Projects performed under another's supervision do not constitute the independent expertise required by the Code. [cite: 98]
rationale.d: Duration alone is insufficient; expertise must be established in the specific field through recognized achievement and consensus. [cite: 98]
rationale.correct: Subordinate experience does not automatically establish the professional consensus and track record needed for a specialization claim. [cite: 90, 98]
rationale.takeaway: Claims to specialization must be substantiated by academic credentials or years of recognized independent experience. [cite: 90, 98]

questions.text: Section 1-d of the Code of Ethical Conduct prohibits architects from using which of the following?

options.text: Paid advertisements or self-laudatory publicity
Factual materials presented through literature describing their work
Industrious application of their work to advance public knowledge
Presentations of the aims and standards of the profession

rationale.b: Factual materials presented in literature describing their work are explicitly permitted under professional communication standards. [cite: 133, 136]
rationale.c: The Code encourages architects to dedicate themselves to creative endeavor and advance public knowledge through их work. [cite: 136, 137]
rationale.d: Presentations regarding the aims and standards of the profession support its dignity and are encouraged activities. [cite: 132, 143]
rationale.correct: Section 1-d prohibits architects from using paid advertisements or self-laudatory, exaggerated, or misleading publicity, emphasizing that success should be merited through industrious application. [cite: 133, 144, 150]
rationale.takeaway: Paid ads are forbidden. Success should be sought through quality and meaningful application of expertise, not solicited personal publicity. [cite: 126, 133]

questions.text: According to Section 1-c of the Code, an architect discovers that a friend is practicing architecture without registration. The architect's obligation is to:

options.text: Remain silent to preserve the friendship
Report the violation to the Board of Architecture
Only report if the friend is causing direct harm to a client
Advise the friend privately and give them time to register

rationale.a: Professional duty and legal compliance take precedence over personal relationships in the context of criminal unlicensed practice. [cite: 111, 144]
rationale.c: Unauthorized practice is a violation regardless of whether harm has been proven; reporting is required upon discovery to safeguard the profession. [cite: 90, 97, 111]
rationale.d: Private advice does not fulfill the professional requirement to observe and uphold government laws and regulations. [cite: 97, 111]
rationale.correct: Section 1-c requires architects to abide by laws and not act detrimentally to the profession; silence about unlicensed practice violates this duty. Under RA 9266, practicing without a license is a criminal act, and the architect's duty necessitates taking action, which ethically includes reporting to the PRBoA. [cite: 85, 90, 97]
rationale.takeaway: Reporting illegal practice is an obligation to the profession and public welfare, which supersedes personal relationships. [cite: 90, 97, 111]

questions.text: An architect observes that building code violations in an ongoing project will not be discovered until occupancy. The client assures the architect that 'the building inspector is a personal friend and will overlook minor issues.' The architect's ethical obligation is to:

options.text: Trust the client's statement and proceed with construction, assuming that minor violations will not impact safety
Report the violations to building authorities and possibly refuse to seal documents
Only report if the violations directly threaten life safety, as minor issues may be resolved later
Consult with the general contractor to determine if violations should be disclosed, considering the potential impact on project timelines

rationale.a: Proceeding with known violations undermines the integrity of the profession and compromises public welfare. [cite: 111, 144]
rationale.c: The duty to observe laws applies to all regulations; all violations damage professional standing regardless of perceived severity. [cite: 97, 111]
rationale.d: Legal and ethical compliance is the architect's independent responsibility and cannot be delegated or compromised. [cite: 97]
rationale.correct: The architect must abide by government laws and regulations and act in the best interest of the profession, which includes ensuring code compliance. [cite: 89, 90, 97]
rationale.takeaway: Personal relationships do not excuse code violations; architects have a non-negotiable duty to maintain legality and safety. [cite: 89, 111, 112]
